title: devbin's new vendor builtin collides with a project handler of the same name at two installs
body:
# 0024: devbin's new vendor builtin collides with a project handler of the same name at two installs

## Tags

vendoring, dispatch, shadowing, naming, cross-estate, baselines

## Summary

`devbin vendor` shipped today (0017). Intent and Intentv2 already had a `vendor` command of their own -- the detector 0017 cites as one of the two consumer-side implementations built in devbin's absence. A project handler shadows a built-in by design (D2/D5), so at those two installs `bin/devbin vendor` runs THEIRS.

Both commands are correct and both are named `vendor`, and **they answer different questions**:

| Command                    | Baseline               | Reports                                       |
| -------------------------- | ---------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| Intent's `vendor` handler  | tree vs MANIFEST       | "28 file(s) MATCH the manifest"               |
| devbin's `vendor` builtin  | tree vs SOURCE         | "28 tracked, 0 divergent -- Level with <src>" |

The first is doctor's question. The second is the question 0017 exists to answer BECAUSE doctor could not: a re-vendor rewrites the files and the manifest together, so tree-vs-manifest cannot see divergence that tree-vs-source can.

## Reproduction

Sweep #3, 2026-08-24, immediately after upgrading Intent to `bf26eb4`:

    cd ~/Devel/prj/Intent && ./bin/devbin vendor
    -> vendored devbin  version 0.1.0
       28 file(s) MATCH the manifest
       no local patches -- this project is running stock devbin.

Devbin's builtin, reached by bypassing resolution:

    PROJECT_ROOT=$p DEVBIN_LIB=$p/bin/.devbin/lib bash $p/bin/.devbin/lib/cmd/vendor
    -> 28 tracked, 0 divergent, 0 unlisted
       Level with /Users/matts/Devel/prj/Devbin.

Same tree, same second, two different questions answered under one word.

## Root Cause

Devbin grew a built-in at a name two consumers had already taken. That is not a defect in the shadowing -- D2 is what lets a project override anything devbin ships, and it is load-bearing -- but issue 0018 is the same shape from the other direction, closed hours earlier: a project handler standing at a built-in name, meaning something else, with nothing announcing the substitution.

The framework has no way to say "this name is now mine too". Nothing warns, nothing lists the collision, and the two commands' outputs look similar enough at a glance to be mistaken for each other.

## Impact

**The immediate cost was nearly a wrong-baseline green banked as a convergence check.** Sweep #3 uses `devbin vendor`'s exit status to assert each install is level with its source. At Intent and Intentv2 that assertion was answered by the handler measuring tree-vs-manifest -- an instrument that cannot see the thing being asserted. It was caught because the output looked unfamiliar and was read rather than skimmed, which is not a control.

The general cost: a consumer reading "vendor says we are clean" now has to know which `vendor` ran, and the two disagree exactly in the case that matters -- an uncommitted re-vendor, where tree-vs-manifest reports stock and tree-vs-source reports the truth.

## How wide is it, measured

Two installs collide (Intent, Intentv2). **Lamplight checked its own tree on being warned and is clear** -- no handler and no config command at that name, only the word in a comment -- and has flagged `vendor` as reserved on its board so nobody mints one tomorrow (lamplight/vc, 2026-08-24). That is the mitigation option A would automate: a peer had to be TOLD, by hand, that a name had been taken upstream, and the other nine installs have not been told.

## Proposed Fix

For hv to size, and worth coordinating with intent/vc since two of the three implementations are theirs.

**A. Devbin announces the shadowing.** `doctor` already knows how to enumerate built-ins and project handlers; a note when a project handler stands at a built-in name would have made this visible the moment it happened, and would equally have caught 0018 eighteen days earlier. Cheap, general, and it names the class rather than this instance.

**B. The consumers retire their handler onto the builtin.** 0017's own resolution left this to each estate. The upstream now answers the stronger question, so the local detector is a Highlander duplicate -- but it is their tree and their call, and Intent's use of devbin is transitional anyway (hv, 2026-08-24).

**C. Rename nothing.** `vendor` is the right name for what devbin ships, and renaming to dodge a collision would leave the general problem -- any built-in can collide with any handler -- unaddressed.

**Recommendation: A, and let B follow at each estate's pace.** A is the only one that closes the class, and the class has now produced two measured instances in one day.

## Related

- 0017 -- shipped the builtin, and named these two consumer implementations as the ones to fold in
- 0018 -- the same collision from the other direction, at devbin's own `check`
- 0023 -- the sweep that surfaced this, and whose convergence assertion it nearly falsified

## Resolutions

**CLOSED 2026-08-24 (vc). hv ruled option A: devbin announces the shadowing.** Not a rename, and not a demand that consumers retire anything -- option A was the only one that closes the CLASS, and the class had produced two measured instances in a single day.

`doctor` gains a `shadowing` check. It compares two lists devbin already keeps -- the built-in catalogue against the project's handlers and config -- and reports every project name standing where devbin ships its own, at both levels: a whole command, and one option of a command that the catalogue implements as `@builtin`. Both levels, because 0018 was both at once (a handler at `check` PLUS `run:` lines on three of its options) and reporting only the command would have named the smaller half.

**A NOTE, never a failure.** Overriding is legal and load-bearing -- D2 and D5 exist precisely so a project can put its own thing at any name devbin ships -- so a doctor going red here would be red on every project using a documented feature, and a check nobody can satisfy is a check nobody reads. It reports its count even at ZERO, because a row that appears only on a hit is indistinguishable from a row that never ran.

**Verified against the thing it was built for.** Run against Intent, the check names the collision this issue is about, along with five other overrides that estate makes deliberately:

    shadowing: 6 project name(s) stand where devbin ships its own
      cli shadows the built-in
      build shadows the built-in
      check format shadows the built-in
      precommit shadows the built-in
      macos shadows the built-in
      vendor shadows the built-in          <- this issue, found automatically

And against devbin itself it immediately names `test` (a handler) and `check critic` (the deliberate corpus divergence declared in 0018's fix) -- both true, both intended, neither previously visible anywhere.

**It would have caught 0018 eighteen days earlier**, which is the real argument for it. That defect was a handler standing at a built-in name from 2026-08-06, found on 08-24 only because two estates compared seal contents by hand.

**A test caught its own author.** The first draft of the command-level test put the handler at `doctor` itself -- so the handler ran INSTEAD of doctor, the check never executed, and the assertion compared two empty strings. The shadowing being real is exactly what made that test unable to observe it. It uses `upgrade` now.

**Not closed by this:** the nine installs that are not Intent still have no way to learn a name has been taken upstream except by being told. This check ships in the vendored half, so it reaches them on their next upgrade -- see the sweep note on the board. Lamplight was told by hand and has reserved the name; that hand-delivery is what this check automates.
